newsitem.title: USA: U.S. trade gap widens, especially with China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. trade gap widens, especially with China.

text.p: Costly oil imports and weak overseas sales of commercial aircraft helped drive the U.S. trade deficit with the rest of the world unexpectedly higher in September, the Commerce Department said on Wednesday.
The deficit climbed 10.1 percent to $11.34 billion from a revised $10.3 billion in August, contrary to Wall Street economists' expectations for a narrowing in the trade gap to $9.5 billion.
A politically controversial shortfall on trade with China continued to swell in September while a small improvement was posted with Japan.
Total exports of goods and services dropped 1.4 percent in September to $68.79 billion while imports increased for a third consecutive month, rising a slight 0.1 percent to $80.13 billion.

"The export side was very bad with a decline of over 0.1 percent versus an expected rise, and it was really based across major categories," Lee Youngdahl, an analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. Inc., said. "Clearly the dollar's strength earlier this year and sluggishness of recovery abroad is weighing on exports."

Commerce said the United States' cumulative deficit on trade for the July-September third quarter of $33.2 billion was the highest in nearly nine years, since it hit $38.6 billion in the fourth quarter of 1987.

A day after a high-level Chinese delegation met U.S. officials to discuss trade and economic issues, Commerce said the third-quarter deficit with China soared to $13.3 billion to surpass the quarterly deficit with Japan of $11.9 billion.
Once again in September, China was the country with which the United States had the biggest bilateral deficit of $4.73 billion, an increase of 0.4 percent from August.
The deficit with Japan eased 0.3 percent to $3.79 billion in September.

"China has definitely surpassed Japan as the highest deficit country. This is going to cause some political rumblings, because we already have representatives over there right now and it's very contentious," Donald Maude, chief U.S. economist at Scotia Capital Markets Inc., said.
"You're going to hear a lot of talk from Congress about China. The Most Favoured Nation trade status may come up for debate again," Maude added.
The United States typically runs a surplus on its trade with other countries in services like travel and tourism that partly offsets big merchandise trade deficits.

"The entire decline and deterioration in the trade deficit was due to a sharp decline in exports, particularly exports of capital goods," Elliott Platt, managing director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp., said.
In September, the merchandise deficit rose 7.6 percent to $17.68 billion from $16.42 billion in August. The surplus on services increased 3.5 percent to $6.34 billion from $6.12 billion in August.

Imports of all types of petroleum products increased 9.3 percent in September to $5.97 billion. The price per barrel of imported crude oil hit $20.02 compared with $18.65 in August -- the highest price since January 1991 during the Gulf War against Iraq, when a barrel of imported oil cost $22.98.
As a result, the monthly deficit with oil-producing OPEC countries soared 27.8 percent to $2.2 billion in September, the highest shortfall since November 1990.

Foreign sales of civilian aircraft plummeted in September, down to $760 million from $1.35 billion in August. Analysts said beforehand that shipments of completed aircraft by Boeing Co. had fallen in September.
Commerce said that imports of industrial supplies and materials hit a record $17.4 billion in September and that consumer goods imports of $14.8 billion also were a record.
On the export side, foreign sales of automobiles, parts and engines were a record $5.9 billion.
The U.S. trade deficit with Western Europe declined in September by 33.6 percent to $1.04 billion from $1.56 billion in August.
Similarly, there was a slight 1.5 percent narrowing in the deficit with Canada to $2.02 billion from $2.38 billion in August.
But the shortfall on trade with Mexico grew 8.9 percent to $1.68 billion in September from $1.54 billion in August.
